llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper introduces Moment Matching Distillation, a novel method to accelerate sampling in diffusion models by distilling multi-step models into few-step versions. This is achieved by matching conditional expectations of clean data given noisy data along the sampling trajectory. The approach extends existing one-step distillation methods to the multi-step setting, reinterpreting them through a moment matching perspective. The distilled models, particularly with up to 8 sampling steps, achieve new state-of-the-art results on ImageNet, outperforming both their one-step counterparts and the original many-step teacher models. The method also demonstrates promising results in fast, high-resolution text-to-image generation directly in image space.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The core methodology involves casting the distribution matching problem as matching conditional expectations of clean data (x) given noisy data (zt) along the diffusion process's sampling trajectory, specifically aiming for Eg[˜x|zs] = Eq[x|zs]. This is achieved by minimizing the L2-distance between these moments. Two variations are proposed: (1) Alternating Optimization: An auxiliary denoising model (gϕ) is trained on samples from the distilled generator (gη) using a standard diffusion loss, with gϕ and gη updated in alternating steps. gϕ is also regularized to stay close to the teacher model (gθ). (2) Parameter-Space Moment Matching: An instantaneous version of the auxiliary model is derived, effectively matching teacher gradients between the training data and generated data in parameter space. This method requires processing two independent minibatches per update. Distilled models sample from the conditional q(zs|˜x, zt). Key hyperparameters include EDM noise schedules and training loss weighting, with adjustments for low-step sampling stability. Adam optimizer with gradient clipping is used, and classifier-free guidance can be applied to the teacher model.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The methods were evaluated on class-conditional image generation using the ImageNet dataset (64x64 and 128x128 resolutions) and on text-to-image generation using a licensed dataset of text-image pairs (512x512 resolution), with zero-shot FID and CLIP Score reported on MS-COCO. A 400 million parameter model based on Simple Diffusion was used for ImageNet, and a UViT model with a T5 XXL text encoder for text-to-image. Base models were trained for 1M steps. Distillation was performed for up to 200,000 steps (ImageNet) or 50,000 steps (text-to-image) with global batch sizes of 2048 and 512, respectively. FID was calculated every 5,000 steps, reporting the optimal FID. Experiments were run on TPUv5e with 256 chips. Base models used slight classifier-free guidance (w=0.1) and optimized sampling noise, while distilled models achieved better FID without guidance (though IS/CLIP improved with it) and used standard ancestral sampling.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The alternating optimization algorithm is generally not guaranteed to converge, similar to GANs. For very few sampling steps (e.g., 1-step), some other existing distillation methods still show better results. The authors acknowledge that automated metrics of image quality (FID, IS, CLIP Score) are highly imperfect. During optimization, moment matching and score matching objectives differ because the approximation pη(zt|zs) ≈ q(zt|zs) is not exact until convergence.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future work includes improving the 1-step sampling results of the proposed method. Further study is planned to understand why moment matching can improve upon the base teacher sampler and to test hypotheses regarding these causes. The authors intend to conduct a full set of human evaluations on the outputs of the distilled models to complement the reported automated metrics. Additionally, there is an interest in exploring the algorithmic space between the alternating optimization and instantaneous parameter-space moment matching versions, aiming for deeper insights into their respective costs and benefits, and guaranteeing fixed point attainment for both methods during optimization.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_code: No directly relevant code for the described method was found in the provided repository content. The repository contains JAX benchmarks, build scripts, educational examples of JAX internals, and implementations of other machine learning models (e.g., Transformer, ADVI, VAE), but not a diffusion model using conditional expectation matching.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_info: No experimental settings or specific details related to the 'Alternating Optimization' or 'Parameter-Space Moment Matching' variations of the diffusion model were found in the provided repository content. The files mostly cover JAX library features, build configurations, and unrelated ML examples.

research_study_list.title: Training-Free Adaptive Diffusion with Bounded Difference Approximation Strategy
research_study_list.abstract:
Diffusion models have recently achieved great success in the synthesis of
high-quality images and videos. However, the existing denoising techniques in
diffusion models are commonly based on step-by-step noise predictions, which
suffers from high computation cost, resulting in a prohibitive latency for
interactive applications. In this paper, we propose AdaptiveDiffusion to
relieve this bottleneck by adaptively reducing the noise prediction steps
during the denoising process. Our method considers the potential of skipping as
many noise prediction steps as possible while keeping the final denoised
results identical to the original full-step ones. Specifically, the skipping
strategy is guided by the third-order latent difference that indicates the
stability between timesteps during the denoising process, which benefits the
reusing of previous noise prediction results. Extensive experiments on image
and video diffusion models demonstrate that our method can significantly speed
up the denoising process while generating identical results to the original
process, achieving up to an average 2~5x speedup without quality degradation.
research_study_list.full_text: Training-Free Adaptive Diffusion with Bounded Difference Approximation Strategy Hancheng Ye1,∗, Jiakang Yuan2,∗, Renqiu Xia3, Xiangchao Yan1, Tao Chen2, Junchi Yan3, Botian Shi1, Bo Zhang1,‡ 1Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory 2School of Information Science and Technology, Fudan University 3School of Artificial Intelligence, Shanghai Jiao Tong University yehancheng@pjlab.org.cn, jkyuan22@m.fudan.edu.cn, zhangbo@pjlab.org.cn Abstract Diffusion models have recently achieved great success in the synthesis of high- quality images and videos. However, the existing denoising techniques in diffusion models are commonly based on step-by-step noise predictions, which suffers from high computation cost, resulting in a prohibitive latency for interactive applications. In this paper, we propose AdaptiveDiffusion to relieve this bottleneck by adaptively reducing the noise prediction steps during the denoising process. Our method considers the potential of skipping as many noise prediction steps as possible while keeping the final denoised results identical to the original full-step ones. Specifically, the skipping strategy is guided by the third-order latent difference that indicates the stability between timesteps during the denoising process, which benefits the reusing of previous noise prediction results. Extensive experiments on image and video diffusion models demonstrate that our method can significantly speed up the denoising process while generating identical results to the original process, achieving up to an average 2 ∼ 5× speedup without quality degradation. The code is available at https://github.com/UniModal4Reasoning/ AdaptiveDiffusion. 1 Introduction Recently, Diffusion models [1, 11, 30, 33] have emerged as a powerful tool for synthesizing high- quality images and videos. Their capability to generate realistic and detailed visual content has made them a popular choice in various applications, ranging from artistic creation to data augmentation,e.g., Midjourney, Sora [4], etc. However, the conventional denoising techniques employed in these models involve step-by-step noise predictions, which are computationally intensive and lead to significant latency, e.g., taking tens seconds for SDXL [ 32] to generate a high-quality image of 1024x1024 resolutions. Diffusion acceleration as an effective technique has been deeply explored recently, which mainly focuses on three paradigms: (1) reducing sampling steps [39, 13, 23, 35, 24], (2) optimizing model architecture [15, 42, 9, 27] and (3) parallelizing inference [16, 38]. Currently, most strategies are designed based on a fixed acceleration mode for all prompt data. However, in our experiments, it is observed that different prompts may require different steps of noise prediction to achieve the same content as the original denoising process, as presented in Fig. 1. Here, we compare the denoising paths using two different prompts for SDXL [32], both of which preserve rich content against the original full-step generation results. The denoising pathdenotes a bool-type sequence, where each element represents whether to infer the noise from the noise prediction model. It can be observed that Prompt 2 needs more steps to generate an almost lossless image than Prompt *Equal contribution, ‡Corresponding author. 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024). arXiv:2410.09873v1  [cs.CV]  13 Oct 2024Two skipping paths for different prompts, which are predicted by our method. For Prompt 1, we only need 20 steps out of 50 steps for noise predictions to generate an almost lossless image, while for Prompt 2, we need 26 steps out of 50 steps to achieve an almost lossless image. 1 (A lower LPIPS [51] value means more similarity between two images generated by the original strategy and our strategy). Therefore, it is necessary to explore a prompt-adaptive acceleration paradigm to consider the denoising diversity between different prompts. Motivated by this observation, in this paper, we deeply dive into the skipping scheme for the noise prediction model and propose AdaptiveDiffusion, a novel approach that adaptively accelerates the generation process according to different input prompts. The fundamental concept behind AdaptiveDiffusion is to adaptively reduce the number of noise prediction steps according to different input prompts during the denoising process, and meanwhile maintain the quality of the final output. The key insight driving our method is that the redundancy of noise prediction is highly related to the third-order differential distribution between temporally-neighboring latents. This relation can be leveraged to design an effective skipping strategy, allowing us to decide when to reuse previous noise prediction results and when to proceed with new calculations. Our approach utilizes the third- order latent difference to assess the redundancy of noise prediction at each timestep, reflecting our strategy’s dependency on input information, thus achieving a prompt-adaptive acceleration paradigm. Extensive experiments conducted on both image and video diffusion models demonstrate the effec- tiveness of AdaptiveDiffusion. The results show that our method can achieve up to a 5.6x speedup in the denoising process with better preservation quality. This improvement in acceleration quality opens up new possibilities for the application of diffusion models in real-time and interactive environments. In summary, AdaptiveDiffusion represents a substantial advancement in adaptively efficient diffusion, offering a practical solution to the challenge of high computational costs associated with sequentially denoising techniques. The main contribution is threefold: (1) To our best knowledge, our method is the first to explore the adaptive diffusion acceleration from the step number reduction of noise predictions that makes different skipping paths for different prompts. (2) We propose a novel approach, namely AdaptiveDiffusion, which develops a plug-and-play criterion to decide whether the noise prediction should be inferred or reused from the previous noise results. (3) Extensive experiments conducted on various diffusion models [ 32, 33, 52, 44] and tasks [ 7, 21, 45, 8] demonstrate the superiority of our AdaptiveDiffusion to the existing acceleration methods in the trade-off among efficiency, performance and generalization ability. 2 Related Works 2.1 Diffusion Models Diffusion models [1, 11, 30, 33, 10] have achieved great success and served as a milestone in content generation. To improve the efficiency of DDPM, Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) [ 33] perform forward and reverse processes in a latent space of lower dimensionality which further evolves into Stable Diffusion (SD) family [ 36, 32]. Recently, video diffusion models [ 3, 52, 2, 44] have attracted increasing attention, especially after witnessing the success of Sora [ 4]. Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) [3] introduces a three-stage training pipeline and obtains a video generation model with strong motion representation. I2VGen-XL [52] first obtains a model with multi-level feature extraction ability, then enhances the resolution and injects temporal information in the second stage. Despite the high quality achieved by diffusion models, the inherent nature of the reverse process which needs high computational cost slows down the inference process. 2.2 Accelerating Diffusion Models Current works accelerate diffusion models can be divided into the following aspects. (1) Reducing Sampling Steps[39, 23, 24, 49, 40, 25, 20, 37, 28, 29, 26]. DDIM [ 39] optimizes sampling steps by exploring a non-Markovian process. Further studies [ 23, 24, 49] such as DPM-Solver [ 23] propose different solvers for diffusion SDEs and ODEs to reduce sampling steps. Another way to optimize sampling steps is to train few-step diffusion models by distillation [ 40, 25, 20]. Among them, consistency models [40, 25] directly map noise to data to enable one-step generation. Other works [20, 37] explore progressive distillation or adversarial distillation to effectively reduce the reverse steps. Besides, some works [26, 42, 29] introduce early stop mechanism into diffusion models. (2) Optimizing Model Architecture[9, 19, 46, 27, 5, 47, 22, 41]. Another strategy to accelerate diffusion models is to optimize model efficiency to reduce the cost during inference. Diff-pruning [9] compresses diffusion models by employing Taylor expansion over pruned timesteps. DeepCache [27] notices the feature redundancy in the denoising process and introduces a cache mechanism to reuse pre-computed features. (3) Parallel Inference[16, 38, 12]. The third line lies in sampling or calculating in a parallel way. ParaDiGMS [38] proposes to use Picard iteration to run multiple steps in parallel. DistriFusion [ 16] introduces displaced patch parallelism by reusing the pre-computed feature maps. Compared with the existing paradigms designing a fixed acceleration mode for all input prompts, our method highlights the adaptive acceleration manner with a plug-and-play criterion based on the high-order latent differential distribution, which allows various diffusion models with different sampling schedulers to achieve significant speedup with a negligible performance drop and deployment cost. 3 The Proposed Approach 3.1 Preliminary Reverse Denoising Process.Diffusion models [11, 39] are designed to learn two processes with noise addition (known as the forward process) and noise reduction (known as the reverse process). 3(a) Noise Pred + Latent Update  @ 50 steps (Full) (b) Noise Pred @ 25 steps (Half) + Latent Update @ 50 steps (Full) (c) Noise Pred + Latent Update  @ 25 steps (Full) (d) Noise Pred + Latent Update  @ 25 steps (Half) Figure 3: Different update strategies. During the inference stage, only the reverse denoising process is adopted that starts from the Gaussian noise xT ∼ N(0, I) and iteratively denoises the input sample under the injected condition to get the final clean image(s) x0, where T is the predefined number of denoising steps. Specifically, given an intermediate noisy image xi at timestep i (i = 1, ..., T), the noise prediction model ϵθ (e.g., UNet [34]) takes xi, timestep ti and an additional condition c (e.g., text, image, and motion embeddings, etc) as input to approximate the noise distribution in xi. The update from xi to xi−1 is determined by different samplers (a.k.a, schedulers) that can be generally formulated as Eq. (1): xi−1 = f(i − 1) · xi − g(i − 1) · ϵθ(xi, ti), i = 1, . . . , T, (1) where f(i) and g(i) are step-related coefficients derived by specific samplers [ 23, 50]. The com- putation in the update process mainly involves a few element-wise additions and multiplications. Therefore, the main computation cost in the denoising process stems from the inference of noise prediction model ϵθ [16]. Step Skipping Strategy.As proved by previous works [27, 42, 15], features between consecutive timesteps present certain similarities in distribution, thus there exists a set of redundant computations that can be skipped. Previous works usually skip either the whole update process or the partial computation within the noise prediction model at redundant timesteps. However, as visualized in Fig. 3, the latent update process in those redundant timesteps may be important to the lossless image generation. Besides, the calculation redundancy of the noise prediction model within each denoising process is still under-explored. To reduce the computation cost from the noise prediction model, we consider directly reducing the number of noise prediction steps from the original denoising process, which will be proved more effective and efficient to accelerate the generation with almost no quality degradation in Sec. 3.3. Given a certain timestep i to skip, our skipping strategy for the update process can be formulated using Eq. (2): xi = f(i) · xi+1 − g(i) · ϵθ(xi+1, ti+1), xi−1 = f(i − 1) · xi − g(i − 1) · ϵθ(xi+1, ti+1). In this section, we take SDXL [ 32] with Euler sampling scheduler as an example to describe the effectiveness of the proposed third-order estimator. Before deriving the third-order estimation criterion, one thing is to calculate the optimal skipping path from the given timestep number, so that we can evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed estimator. Considering the explosive searching cost within a large search space ( e.g., searching the optimal path of skipping N steps within T steps for one prompt requires CN T search time cost), we design a greedy search algorithm to approximate the optimal skipping path under different skipping targets, which can be found in Alg. (1). Here we randomly take the prompt “A bustling 18th-century market scene with vendors, shoppers, and cobblestone streets, all depicted in the detailed oil painting style." as an example to visualize the optimal skipping path searched by the greedy search algorithm under the predefined skipping target constraint. Meanwhile, as the skipping error is upper-bounded by the constraint of the first- order latent difference, it inspires us to explore the relationship between the first-order difference distribution and the ideal skipping path. As shown in Fig. 4, we visualize two types of first-order difference (one in Fig. 4a representing the noise difference distribution, another in Fig. 4b representing latent difference distribution) in the original full-step diffusion to compare with the skipping path. It can be observed that both two distributions of first-order differences are smooth across the denoising process, showing little relationship with the optimal skipping path. A similar insight can be observed in the distribution of the second-order latent difference, as shown in Fig. 4b. However, when considering the third-order latent difference distribution, it presents a significant fluctuation in the original full-step denoising process. As shown in Fig. 4c, the distribution of the skipping path is related to the distribution of the third-order latent difference, especially in the early denoising process (around 15 timesteps), where the noise densely updates when the third-order latent difference increases and can be skipped when the third-order difference decreases. As for the later denoising process, when most third-order differences are relatively minor, most noise prediction steps are also skipped. According to the first-order latent difference presented in Fig. 4b, the differences between consecutive latent in the early denoising process are significantly larger than those in the later denoising process. Therefore, the precise importance estimation of noise predictions in the early process is much more important and the third-order difference distribution can intuitively serve as the indicator of the noise prediction strategy. The theoretical relation between the third-order derivative of latents and the optimal skipping scheme is analyzed in Appendix A.2.4. Criterion. We conduct experiments in three prompt-based settings including text-to-image (T2I), image- to-video (I2V), and text-to-video (T2V) generation tasks. In addition, we also test the effectiveness of AdaptiveDiffusion on the conditional image generation task. For the T2I task, we use Stable Diffusion-v1-5 (SD-1-5) [33] and Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) [32] and evaluate on three different sampling schedulers (i.e., DDIM [39], DPM-Solver++ [24], and Euler). For the I2V and T2V tasks, we utilize I2VGen-XL [52] and ModelScopeT2V [44] respectively. Note that we use ZeroScope-v2 instead of the original ModelScopeT2V model to generate watermark-free videos. For conditional image generation, we use LDM-4 [33] as the baseline model. Benchmark Datasets.Following [27], we use ImageNet [7] and MS-COCO 2017 [21] to evaluate the results on class-conditional image generation and T2I tasks, respectively. For the I2V task, we randomly sample 100 prompts and reference images in AIGCBench [ 8]. For the T2V task, we conduct experiments on a widely-used benchmark MSR-VTT [45] and sample one caption for each video in the validation set as the test prompt. More details can be found in Appendix A.3. Comparison Baselines.We compare AdaptiveDiffusion against DeepCache and Adaptive DPM- Solver in both generation quality and efficiency. Deepcache [27] caches high-level features of UNet to update the low-level features at each denoising step, thus reducing the computational cost of UNet. The latter [23] dynamically adjusts the step size by combining different orders of DPM-Solver. Evaluation Metrics.For all tasks, we evaluate our proposed method in both quality and efficiency. A.1 Limitations and Broader Impacts Currently, AdaptiveDiffusion is only evaluated on image generation and video generation tasks. A long-term vision is to achieve lossless acceleration on any modalities generation such as 3D and speech. A.3 Experimental Details A.3.1 More Evaluation Details Statistical Analysis of the Estimated Skipping Path.In Fig. 5, we aim to evaluate the correlation between the estimated skipping paths by our method and the searched optimal skipping paths under different target skipping numbers. This evaluation is crucial to validate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately 16predicting skipping paths. The paths are represented as sequences of binary choices (0 for a skipping step, 1 for a non-skipping step) at each timestep. We employ a χ2 test of independence to assess the statistical correlation between the estimated and optimal paths. We first randomly select several prompts from the test set and use the greedy search algorithm to greedily search the optimal skipping paths under different skipping target steps. For the estimated skipping paths, we discard the setting of Cmax to test the effectiveness of the third-order estimation without regularization and refine the threshold δ in a wide range to achieve various skipping paths with different skipping step numbers. Then, for each skipping step number, we construct a 2×2 contingency table from the searched optimal skipping paths and the estimated skipping paths, with the same skipping step numbers. Finally, using the contingency table, we compute the χ2 statistics and the corresponding p-value to assess the independence between the estimated and the searched optimal skipping paths. Evaluation Tools and Details.Following [16], we use TorchMetrics * to calculate PSNR and LPIPS, and use CleanFID [31]† to calculate FID. Since our method is an adaptive method which means it can choose a suitable skipping path for different prompts, we set batch size to 1 during evaluation. The MACs reported in our experiments are the total MACs in the denoising process following [16]. Besides, the reported MACs, speedup ratio, and latency are the average over the whole dataset. CodeBase. For a fair comparison, when compared with Adaptive DPM-Solver, we use the official codebase of DPM-Solver‡. Experiments for LDM-4-G are based on the official LDM codebase§ and DeepCache codebase¶. Other experiments are based on Diffusers||. Details of Reproduced DeepCache. In this paper, we mainly compare our AdaptiveDiffusion with DeepCache. To ensure the generation quality, we set cache_interval=3 and cache_branch_id=3 for SD-v1-5, SDXL, and ModelScope. Since the memory cost will be largely improved on video generation tasks es- pecially high-resolution tasks (e.g., I2VGen-XL), We set cache_interval=3 and cache_branch_id=0 to reduce the memory costs. For class-conditional image generation task, we follow the official setting and set cache_interval=10. Compared with the ODE solver, the SDE solver includes an additional noise item for the latent update, which is unpredictable by previous randomly generated noises. When the magnitude of random noise is not ignorable, the third-order derivative of the neighboring latents cannot accurately evaluate the difference between the neighboring noise predictions. Therefore, to apply our *https://github.com/Lightning-AI/torchmetrics †https://github.com/GaParmar/clean-fid ‡https://github.com/LuChengTHU/dpm-solver §https://github.com/CompVis/latent-diffusion ¶https://github.com/horseee/DeepCache ||https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers 17method to SDE solvers, we should design an additional indicator that decides whether the randomly generated noise is minor enough or relatively unchanged to trigger the third-order estimator. In this case, we design an additional third-order estimator for the scaled randomly generated noise. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper introduces AdaptiveDiffusion, a novel training-free approach that adaptively accelerates diffusion model generation by reducing noise prediction steps. It is the first method to explore prompt-adaptive diffusion acceleration by creating different skipping paths for various prompts. A key contribution is the development of a plug-and-play criterion based on the third-order latent difference, which effectively identifies computational redundancy and decides when to reuse previous noise prediction results. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AdaptiveDiffusion achieves significant speedups (up to 5.6x) while maintaining generation quality across various image and video diffusion models and tasks, outperforming existing acceleration methods in efficiency, performance, and generalization.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: AdaptiveDiffusion addresses the high computational cost of diffusion models by adaptively reducing the number of noise prediction steps. The method operates on the principle that the redundancy of noise prediction correlates with the third-order differential distribution between temporally-neighboring latents. It utilizes a third-order estimator that takes current and previous latents as input to decide if the next noise prediction can be skipped, formulated by the criterion: ξ(xi−1) = ∆(3)xi−1 ≥ δ∥∆xi∥, where ∆(3)xi−1 is the third-order latent difference and δ is a threshold. If the criterion indicates a skip (ξ returns False), the noise from the previous step is reused. A hyperparameter Cmax (maximum continuous skipping steps) is also introduced to control the accumulation of errors. The method is training-free and designed as a plug-and-play criterion for various diffusion models and sampling schedulers. For SDE solvers, an additional indicator for scaled randomly generated noise is designed.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on various prompt-based generation tasks: text-to-image (T2I), image-to-video (I2V), text-to-video (T2V), and conditional image generation. Models evaluated include Stable Diffusion-v1-5 (SD-1-5) and Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) with DDIM, DPM-Solver++, and Euler schedulers for T2I; I2VGen-XL for I2V; ModelScopeT2V (ZeroScope-v2) for T2V; and LDM-4 for conditional image generation. Unconditional image generation was also tested on CIFAR10 and LSUN. Benchmark datasets used are ImageNet and MS-COCO 2017 for image tasks, AIGCBench (100 random prompts/images) for I2V, and MSR-VTT for T2V. Baselines for comparison were DeepCache and Adaptive DPM-Solver. Evaluation metrics included MACs, latency, and speedup ratio for efficiency; PSNR, LPIPS, and FID for image quality; and per-frame PSNR, LPIPS, and FVD for video quality. All experiments were performed on RTX 3090 GPUs, with varying original sampling timesteps (e.g., T=50 for SD-1-5/SDXL, T=250 for LDM-4) and adjusted hyperparameters δ and Cmax for each model and task. Statistical correlation between estimated and optimal skipping paths was assessed using a χ² test of independence.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: AdaptiveDiffusion has primarily been evaluated on image and video generation tasks, indicating a need for broader validation across other modalities. The method may not be effective for extreme few-step generation settings due to the rapid and significant changes in latent features during such early denoising stages.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: A long-term research direction is to extend AdaptiveDiffusion to achieve lossless acceleration for generation across a wider range of modalities beyond images and videos, such as 3D content and speech generation.

def sample_from_quad_center(total_numbers, n_samples, center, pow=1.2):
    while pow > 1:
        # Generate linearly spaced values between 0 and a max value
        x_values = np.linspace((-center)**(1/pow), (total_numbers-center)**(1/pow), n_samples+1)
        indices = [0] + [x+center for x in np.unique(np.int32(x_values**pow))[1:-1]]
        if len(indices) == n_samples:
            break
        pow -=0.02
    if pow <= 1:
        raise ValueError("Cannot find suitable pow. Please adjust n_samples or decrease center.")
    return indices, pow

        interval_seq = sorted(interval_seq)
        #print(interval_seq, len(interval_seq), pow)

        with self.progress_bar(total=num_inference_steps) as progress_bar:
            #print("[INFO] Update Feature Interval = {}, Update Layer Number = {}, Update Block Number = {}".format(cache_interval, cache_layer_id, cache_block_id))
            for i, t in enumerate(timesteps):
                # expand the latents if we are doing classifier free guidance
                latent_model_input = torch.cat([latents] * 2) if do_classifier_free_guidance else latents
                latent_model_input = self.scheduler.scale_model_input(latent_model_input, t)

                if i in interval_seq:
                    prv_features = None            

                # predict the noise residual
                noise_pred, prv_features = self.unet(
                    latent_model_input,
                    t,
                    encoder_hidden_states=prompt_embeds,
                    cross_attention_kwargs=cross_attention_kwargs,
                    replicate_prv_feature=prv_features,
                    quick_replicate= cache_interval>1,
                    cache_layer_id=cache_layer_id,
                    cache_block_id=cache_block_id,
                    return_dict=False,
                )

                # perform guidance
                if do_classifier_free_guidance:
                    noise_pred_uncond, noise_pred_text = noise_pred.chunk(2)
                    noise_pred = noise_pred_uncond + guidance_scale * (noise_pred_text - noise_pred_uncond)

                if do_classifier_free_guidance and guidance_rescale > 0.0:
                    # Based on 3.4. in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.08891.pdf
                    noise_pred = rescale_noise_cfg(noise_pred, noise_pred_text, guidance_rescale=guidance_rescale)

                # compute the previous noisy sample x_t -> x_t-1
                latents = self.scheduler.step(noise_pred, t, latents, **extra_step_kwargs, return_dict=False)[0]
                latents_list.append(latents)

                # call the callback, if provided
                if i == len(timesteps) - 1 or ((i + 1) > num_warmup_steps and (i + 1) % self.scheduler.order == 0):
                    progress_bar.update()
                    if callback is not None and i % callback_steps == 0:
                        callback(i, t, latents)

        # ... (rest of the pipeline call method omitted for brevity)
llm_extracted_info.experimental_info:
The method, referred to as "DeepCache" in the repository, accelerates diffusion models by caching and reusing intermediate features within the UNet, rather than skipping full noise prediction steps or applying a third-order estimator as implied by the "AdaptiveDiffusion" description. It is a training-free, plug-and-play criterion.

**Mechanism:**
1.  **`DeepCacheSDHelper`**: This class acts as a wrapper, enabling or disabling the caching mechanism. It intercepts the forward calls of the UNet and its internal blocks.
2.  **Skipping Schedule (`cache_interval`, `uniform`, `pow`, `center`)**: At each inference step, a decision is made whether to perform a full computation (`slow path`) or to reuse cached features (`quick path`).
    *   `cache_interval`: Defines the frequency of full computations. For example, `cache_interval=3` means every 3rd step performs a full computation.
    *   `uniform`: If True, the full computation steps are uniformly distributed (`0, cache_interval, 2*cache_interval, ...`).
    *   `pow`, `center`: If `uniform` is False, `sample_from_quad_center` generates a non-uniform distribution of full computation steps, allowing more frequent full computations at certain stages (e.g., later stages).
3.  **Feature Caching and Reuse (`cache_layer_id`, `cache_block_id`, `replicate_prv_feature`, `quick_replicate`)**:
    *   During a 'slow path' (full computation step), the intermediate feature map from a specified `cache_layer_id` and `cache_block_id` within the UNet's upsampling path is saved as `prv_feature`.
    *   During a 'quick path' (skipped computation step), the UNet's forward pass is modified (`quick_replicate=True`). It partially recomputes the downsampling path up to `cache_layer_id` and `cache_block_id` (or just prior to it), and then directly uses the `replicate_prv_feature` to reconstruct the remaining upsampling path, effectively skipping a significant portion of computation.

**Experimental Settings/Hyperparameters (examples from code):**
*   `cache_interval`: Integer, typically 3 or 5. Controls the frequency of full computations.
*   `cache_branch_id`: Integer, ranging from 0 to (num_down_blocks * num_blocks_per_down_block). It specifies which specific block's output within the UNet (calculated as `cache_layer_id = cache_branch_id % 3` and `cache_block_id = cache_branch_id // 3`) to cache for reuse.
*   `uniform`: Boolean, `True` for uniform skipping, `False` for non-uniform.
*   `pow`: Float (e.g., 1.4), used in `sample_from_quad_center` to shape non-uniform skipping intervals.
*   `center`: Integer (e.g., 15), used in `sample_from_quad_center` to shift the distribution of non-uniform skipping intervals.
*   `seed`: Integer (e.g., 42), for reproducibility.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: 1. Current accelerators either assume a fixed, single-device context or treat device-migration as an all-or-nothing hand-off. There is no fine-grained routing of individual solver steps (or even spatial tiles) to the most suitable processor under constantly-changing bandwidth, thermal and privacy constraints.
2. Existing cross-backbone warm-starts rely on a linear Koopman map fitted on the fly. When the target backbone diverges strongly in architecture (e.g. video diffusion with temporal convolutions, or depth-conditioned ControlNet) a single linear map is often insufficient, forcing re-initialisation and quality loss.
3. Kalman / Parareal feature reuse has so far been exploited only for arithmetic efficiency; the communication cost of sending those reused features across WAN or Bluetooth is now the dominant latency when phones collaborate with cloud or wearables.
4. Quantisation and skipping are still designed at tensor granularity. However, the memory-bandwidth bottleneck on mobile NPUs is dominated by a handful of large attention tiles; no scheduler reasons at tile-level while also accounting for network transfer cost.
5. Current privacy and fairness monitors flush the whole cache when a statistical test fails, which hurts UX. A more surgical mitigation that perturbs only the offending channels or tiles is missing.
Methods: We propose ORCHID-D⁴: Orchestrated, Hierarchical, Differentially-private, Distributed Diffusion.
A. Step-Level Dynamic Off-Loading (SL-DO). We formalise inference as a Mixed-Integer Program that assigns every solver step t and every 32×32 latent tile τ to one of M heterogeneous devices. The objective minimises end-to-end latency plus an energy–privacy regulariser. The cost coefficients are profiled online (using micro-benchmarks and measured network RTT) and the MIP is re-solved every 0.5 s via a warm-started branch-and-bound on the phone’s little cores (≤3 ms).
B. Piece-wise Koopman Adapter (PKA). Instead of one global linear Φ we learn a small dictionary of K piece-wise linear maps {Φ_k}. A decision tree, trained once on open-source backbones and then pruned to 8-KB, selects Φ_k based on layer depth, channel group and condition type. At run-time only the chosen Φ_k is fine-tuned with recursive least squares, preserving cross-backbone reuse even for video or depth branches.
C. Hierarchical Rényi-Coded State (HRCS). The SP-HKF state is entropy-coded with a learnt Gaussian-mixture prior and split into three tiers: (1) 96-byte per-tile mean, (2) optional 4-bit low-rank basis, (3) optional eigen-noise seeds. SL-DO may decide to migrate only tier-1 for slow links (BLE) and reconstruct higher tiers locally with a calibrated noise injector, cutting average transmitted bytes by 4.6×.
D. Tile-Aware Quant-Skip (TAQS). Attention maps are partitioned into 8×8 tiles; each tile carries a skip-probability π and a candidate bit-width b∈{4,8,16}. A bi-criteria knapsack packs tiles into the on-chip SRAM budget while maximising ( expected quality gain − λ·transfer_cost ). TAQS is solved greedily in <0.8 ms and feeds its decision back to SL-DO so that communication and memory trade-offs are globally consistent.
E. Channel-Selective Fairness Noise (CF-Noise). When the chi-square monitor detects over-fitting on a protected attribute, only the top-p offending channels (ranked by Rényi contribution) are reset to fresh Gaussian noise; the rest of the cache stays. This reduces cache flush frequency by 8× while capping leakage at the same δ.
Experimental Setup: Backbones: SD-XL-1.0, Stable Diffusion 3-Medium, ControlNet-Depth, Stable Video Diffusion-XT, AnimateDiff-Canny.
Devices: Pixel 8 Pro (TPU), Meta Quest 3 (AR-SoC), MacBook M3-Max GPU, RTX 4090, AWS A10G.
Workloads: 80 single-prompt sessions, 40 image→video branches, 30 live AR sketch edits, 24 device-handoff traces (phone↔headset↔cloud).
Baselines: H3KF-Diff, DynaDiff-KPG, AsyncDiff (4 GPU), DeepCache+NDTC, SRDS-25.
Metrics: wall-clock latency, transmitted KB per step, energy/J, DRAM GB/s, sFID / sFVD, fairness KL, privacy MI, MOS from 40 users.
Ablations: disable SL-DO; single Φ vs PKA; HRCS tier-1 only; TAQS off; CF-Noise replaced by full flush.
Expected Result: • End-to-end latency 54 ms per 1024² image on Pixel-cloud pair (-1.6× vs DynaDiff-KPG, ‑2.9× vs H3KF-Diff).
• Average wireless data per prompt 32 KB (-78%).
• Energy per frame on headset ‑42%; phone remains below 38 °C in a 3-min AR edit.
• Backbone switch reuse success rate 97% (first SVD frame 95 ms vs 240 ms cold).
• Tile-aware scheduler reduces DRAM bandwidth by 46 %; SM occupancy 93 %.
• Cache flush rate 0.3 % of sessions (8× fewer) while fairness KL < 0.004.
• User MOS equals cloud-only baseline in 87 % comparisons.
Expected Conclusion: ORCHID-D⁴ generalises diffusion acceleration from a single trusted GPU to a fully distributed, privacy-aware orchestration across phones, wearables and cloud. By jointly optimising where (device), what (tile/step) and how (bit-width/skip) computations run, it slashes both latency and wireless bandwidth without retraining. Piece-wise Koopman adapters and channel-selective fairness noise ensure quality and equity even across divergent backbones. These results advocate for treating diffusion inference as a network-aware scheduling problem, opening a new avenue that bridges systems optimisation, information theory and responsible generative AI.

idea.open_problems: Current training-free speed-up techniques for latent-space image diffusion (encoder propagation, DeepCache, AdaptiveDiffusion, etc.) work well when 20-50 solver steps are allowed, but they break down in the extreme-few–step regime (≤10) that is mandatory for real-time applications. Quality loss is mainly caused by naive re-use of stale encoder features: when guidance is strong or textures are complex, small linear drifts between consecutive steps accumulate and the decoder cannot correct them. The key unsolved problem is therefore: How can we reuse encoder (or transformer) representations for many consecutive skipped steps without letting the approximation error explode, while keeping the method training-free and universally applicable to existing checkpoints?
idea.methods: We propose Error-Bounded Feature Extrapolation (EBFE). 1) Local linear dynamical model – For every encoder block we fit a first-order linear predictor online:  ĥt+Δ = A·ht   where A is estimated from two most recent key steps (t−Δ,t). 2) Uncertainty tracker – Together with A we maintain a scalar confidence σ that upper-bounds ‖ĥ−h‖.  σ is obtained analytically from the residual of the last fit and propagated forward. 3) Adaptive horizon – During inference we allow the block to be skipped for up to K steps as long as σ < ϵ, where ϵ is a user-chosen quality knob. 4) Residual corrector – When σ ≥ ϵ we perform a normal forward pass (key step) and update (A,σ). 5) Decoder reuse – As in FasterDiffusion, multiple decoder invocations corresponding to the skipped steps are executed in parallel once their (extrapolated) encoder features are ready. 6) Compatibility layer – EBFE is implemented as a light-weight PyTorch “FeatureExtrapolator” wrapper; it requires no retraining, no change to weight tensors, and co-exists with DPM-Solver, DDIM, etc. Compared with previous work, EBFE introduces (i) an error-bounded predictor rather than blind caching, (ii) a per-block adaptive horizon, and (iii) a mathematically derived quality guarantee (σ ≤ ϵ implies an upper bound on FID drift that can be pre-computed).
idea.experimental_setup: Models & tasks: Stable Diffusion 1.5, SD-XL, DeepFloyd-IF stage-II, DiT-XL (ImageNet 256), all in FP16. 20 text prompts × 500 MS-COCO captions (t2i), and DreamBooth personalised generation. Solvers: DDIM-50, DPM-Solver++(10,8,5 steps). Baselines: DDIM/DPM (no skip), FasterDiffusion, DeepCache, AdaptiveDiffusion, AsyncDiff (4 GPUs). Metrics: FID, sFID, CLIP-score, LPIPS to 50-step reference, runtime (ms/image) on one A100, peak VRAM. Ablations: ϵ∈{0.01,0.02,0.05}, horizon K∈{4,8,16}. Robustness: guidance scale 7.5 vs 12, ControlNet edge conditioning, DreamBooth with 4 fine-tune images.
idea.expected_result: At 8 solver steps EBFE achieves:  – 1.9× speed-up over vanilla DDIM-8 and 1.4× over FasterDiffusion; – FID within +0.15 of DDIM-8 and better than DeepCache (by −0.4); – LPIPS to 50-step reference ≤0.035 (vs 0.06 for DeepCache); – Memory overhead <10 %.  Quality gracefully degrades when ϵ increases, matching user-specified bound; with ϵ=0.01 EBFE retains quality even at 5 steps, where other training-free methods fail.
idea.expected_conclusion: The study will show that error-bounded online extrapolation of encoder features enables the first training-free, quality-preserving acceleration of latent diffusion models in the extreme-few–step regime. EBFE closes the gap between heuristic caching and costly distillation, offering a new knob (ϵ) for continuous speed–quality trade-off. Because the approach is purely run-time, it can be combined with distillation, quantisation, model parallelism, etc., opening a pathway to sub-100 ms text-to-image generation on a single GPU. Future work may extend EBFE to discrete text diffusion and to video diffusion where temporal coherence imposes even stricter error bounds.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Existing training-free accelerators (FasterDiffusion, DeepCache, AdaptiveDiffusion, DeepCache-like block caching) either (1) reuse encoder features blindly with a fixed cadence, (2) cache whole transformer blocks, or (3) decide step–skipping from latent-space heuristics.  None of them  • build a predictive dynamical model of feature evolution,  • attach a formal, per-block error estimate, or  • adapt the caching horizon on-line with a provable upper-bound on quality loss.  The proposed EBFE fits a local linear map A on-the-fly for every encoder block, propagates an analytic confidence σ, and skips computation only while σ≤ε, permitting many consecutive skips even under strong guidance.  This error-bounded extrapolation plus parallel decoder scheduling is absent from the cited works and directly targets the extreme-few-step (≤10) regime where prior cache methods degrade, therefore introducing a qualitatively new idea.
evaluate.significance_reason: If EBFE truly keeps FID and LPIPS almost unchanged at 5–8 solver steps while doubling throughput without retraining, it closes the large practical gap between heuristic caching (fast but quality-lossy) and full distillation (accurate but expensive and checkpoint-specific).  This enables real-time text-to-image (<100 ms) on a single GPU, benefits interactive or on-device use cases, and remains compatible with orthogonal speed-ups (quantisation, distillation, model parallelism).  Academically, providing a bounded-error feature predictor links numerical analysis with network internals and could inspire principled reuse strategies for video or discrete text diffusion.  Impact is therefore substantial, though limited to inference efficiency rather than generation capabilities per se.

idea.open_problems:
1. Existing feature–reuse schemes collapse when fewer than ~8 solver steps are used, mainly because a single linear guess cannot simultaneously track (i) low-frequency structure that changes slowly and (ii) high-frequency details that drift quickly under strong CFG, ControlNet, or DreamBooth perturbations.
2. Confidence scalars per block are too coarse: localised errors (e.g. at edges) explode while the global ℓ2 bound still looks small, forcing frequent key-steps and killing speed-up.
3. Current methods ignore cross-block and cross-scale correlations – predicting each feature tensor independently wastes information embedded in the U-Net hierarchy.
4. Extra memory for long-horizon caches (≥16 skips) becomes the new bottleneck on consumer GPUs.
5. No public benchmark exists for real-time (<100 ms) T2I with large-scale SD-XL or DiT under extreme CFG (≥12) and ControlNet – we lack evidence that any training-free technique can handle this setting.
idea.methods:
We propose Kalman Diffusion Reuse (KaDiR): a multi-scale, probabilistic feature-extrapolation framework.
a) Hierarchical State Space Model – For every resolution level l we learn on-the-fly a linear–Gaussian dynamical system   h^{l}_{t+1}=A^{l}h^{l}_{t}+∑_{k<l}B^{lk}(h^{k}_{t}-Ĉ^{lk}\hat h^{k}_{t})+w^{l}_{t}.  Cross-scale terms B^{lk} inject coarse-to-fine context so that fine-grid detail is steered by low-frequency motion.
b) Kalman Predictor–Corrector – We propagate mean \hat h and covariance Σ through skipped steps; whenever the predicted image-space error \hat ε_FID(Σ) exceeds ε we trigger a correction pass.  The Kalman gain naturally produces a spatial uncertainty map, letting us update only 8×8 tiles whose error > ε_tile (selective decoding).
c) Frequency-Selective Low-Rank Update – Instead of storing full Σ (O(C^2)), we maintain a rank-r covariance in DCT space; r=8 suffices, cutting VRAM by 40-60 %.
d) Coupled Momentum Solver – Combine KaDiR with Heavy-Ball DPM-Solver++ so that solver instabilities and feature-drift are damped coherently; momentum parameters are chosen from the Kalman damping ratio ζ.
e) Zero-copy Cache Compression – Cached features are quantised to 8-bit with NDTC PTQ and packed in shared GPU memory; decompression latency <0.02 ms.
f) Universal Plug-in – Implemented as a PyTorch TorchDynamo graph transform; two lines of code enable KaDiR for any UNet/Transformer backbone.
idea.experimental_setup:
Models: SD 1.5, SD-XL-1.0, DeepFloyd-IF-II, DiT-XL/2 256, and StableVideoDiffusion-XT.
Tasks:  
• 300 MS-COCO prompts (random) + 100 hard prompts (obj + style)  
• DreamBooth personalised generation (8 identities)  
• ControlNet-Canny & ControlNet-Depth (50 images)  
• 16-frame video with Text-to-Video-Zero.
Solvers: DPM-Solver++(5,8), DEIS-10, HB-GHVB-15.
Baselines: vanilla solver, FasterDiffusion, DeepCache, AdaptiveDiffusion (δ tuned), AsyncDiff (4 GPU), EBFE (original single-scale).
Metrics: runtime (ms) single A100 & RTX 4090; peak VRAM; FID-50k vs 50-step reference; tile-wise sFID heat-map; LPIPS; CLIP; temporal FVD (video); number of GPU function calls; energy usage (nvidia-smi).
Ablations: rank r∈{4,8,16}; ε∈{0.01,0.02,0.05}; with/without cross-scale B; momentum on/off; 4-bit cache.
idea.expected_result:
• At 5 solver steps KaDiR reaches 2.3× (A100) / 1.9× (4090) speed-up over DDIM-5, 1.6× over EBFE, with ΔFID≤0.12 on SD-XL.
• Under CFG = 12 + ControlNet edge, quality loss <0.3 FID while DeepCache degrades by 1.1.
• Selective decoding updates only 27 % of tiles on average, cutting decoder FLOPs by 45 %.
• VRAM overhead <6 % thanks to low-rank + 8-bit cache.
• Kalman gain visualisations correlate (ρ=0.78) with true error heat-maps, validating spatial uncertainty.
• Video experiment: KaDiR+HB-15 delivers 16-frame 512² clip in 420 ms with FVD 285 (baseline 1000 ms / 280).
idea.expected_conclusion: KaDiR demonstrates that a probabilistic, multi-scale state-space treatment of latent features enables the first training-free diffusion acceleration that (i) preserves image quality at ≤5 solver steps, (ii) remains stable under extreme CFG and conditioning, and (iii) fits into consumer-GPU memory.  By unifying Kalman prediction, frequency-selective uncertainty, and momentum-stable solvers, KaDiR turns the sequential denoiser into an anytime, spatially-adaptive process, narrowing the gap to distillation while keeping one single universal checkpoint.  The framework opens new research on Bayesian analysis of network internals and on tile-adaptive rendering for video, 3-D, and mobile diffusion.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Most existing training-free speed-up schemes either 1) skip UNet sub-graphs deterministically (FasterDiff, DeepCache), 2) adapt the number of solver steps via heuristic error bounds (AdaptiveDiffusion, EBFE), or 3) accelerate the ODE itself by improved solvers / momentum (DPM-HB, DEIS, STSP).  None of them maintains and propagates an explicit uncertainty estimate of the skipped latent features.  KaDiR frames feature reuse as a linear–Gaussian state-space problem and applies an online Kalman predictor–corrector per UNet scale, propagating both mean and low-rank covariance across skipped steps.  The Kalman gain is then used (i) to decide when a global correction pass is needed and (ii) to trigger spatially selective 8×8-tile decoding – a mechanism absent from prior works.  Cross-scale coupling terms B^{lk} further exploit the hierarchical nature of UNet features, which previous single-scale caches ignore.  Finally, coupling the Kalman damping ratio with Heavy-Ball parameters yields a principled way to stabilise aggressive 5-step solvers, something earlier momentum papers did not tie to feature reuse.  This probabilistic, multi-scale, tile-adaptive reuse pipeline is not present in the listed related works and therefore constitutes clear methodological novelty.
evaluate.significance_reason: If the reported numbers hold, KaDiR delivers (a) sub-100 ms text-to-image on SD-XL/DiT with only 5 solver steps, (b) <0.3 FID degradation under extreme CFG+ControlNet where current caches break, and (c) <6 % VRAM overhead thanks to low-rank 8-bit caching.  Achieving real-time generation on consumer GPUs without any retraining would have immediate practical impact for interactive graphics, mobile apps, and personalised creation.  Academically, introducing state-space estimation and uncertainty-driven spatial adaptation opens a new line of Bayesian analysis inside diffusion networks, potentially influencing future work on video, 3-D and edge deployment.  The contribution is therefore of high but not paradigm-shifting significance.

idea.open_problems: 1. Current feature-reuse methods fail in the ≤5-step, high-guidance regime because they treat each U-Net block independently and propagate only a point estimate of the hidden state. 2. Covariance tracking is either absent or limited to per-block scalars, so localised error bursts cannot be detected soon enough. 3. Cross-scale correlations and long-range temporal patterns (e.g. periodic drift over several skipped steps) are ignored. 4. Memory and bandwidth, not FLOPs, become the dominant bottleneck on consumer GPUs once >8 skips are cached. 5. There is still no public, reproducible benchmark that stresses real-time (<100 ms) inference under strong classifier-free guidance (CFG≥12), multi-condition ControlNet and DreamBooth. 6. Lack of theoretical understanding: existing speed-up rules are heuristic, with no guarantee that the skipped process remains numerically stable under extreme step sizes.
idea.methods:
We propose H3KF-Diff (Hierarchical Koopman–Kalman–Kronecker Forecasting for Diffusion) – a training-free, information-theoretic framework that generalises Kalman Diffusion Reuse.

A. Koopman-Linear Prediction.  For every scale l we fit on-the-fly a low-rank Koopman operator K^l that evolves the joint encoder–decoder feature Z_t=[h^l_t, d^l_t].  Unlike the pure linear model in KaDiR, a learned eigen-basis Φ^l≈PCA(ΔZ) is updated with O(1) incremental SVD per key frame, capturing slowly changing non-linear drift within a fixed linear dynamical system.

B. Kronecker-Structured Covariance.  We approximate Σ_t as (A⊗B)+εI where A encodes channel correlations (rank ≤ 8) and B encodes spatial 8×8-tile correlations (rank ≤ 6).  This gives pixel-accurate uncertainty maps at <4 % VRAM overhead and admits closed-form Kalman updates.

C. Mutual-Information Key-Frame Scheduler.  Instead of a fixed error scalar ε, we compute I_t=I(Ẑ_t;Z_t|Σ_t) via the differential entropy of the Gaussian predictive distribution.  A new key frame is triggered when I_t drops below a target bitrate budget β (user knob), yielding provable upper bounds on image KL divergence and making the method model-agnostic.

D. Bayesian Momentum Coupling.  We derive Heavy-Ball and Nesterov parameters (γ,ζ) from the discretised Kalman transition matrix, guaranteeing A-stability for any step size ≤N/4 where N is the number of UNet residual blocks.  This links numerical ODE stability with feature-reuse theory and removes the need for manual momentum tuning.

E. Memory-Elastic Caching.  We store Φ^l and the first r principal coefficients in 6-bit log-quantised form.  A GPU warp-wide cooperative kernel decompresses one 8×8 tile in 6 clock cycles.  The cache grows/shrinks on-line to respect a user-defined  VRAM cap.

F. OpenRT-Diff Benchmark.  We contribute a public suite with 1 000 prompts, 200 ControlNet images, 12 DreamBooth identities and 8 video scripts, plus reference scripts for SD-XL and DiT.  Metrics include latency, energy, sFID heat-maps, tile-wise information loss, and bitrate of uncertainty maps.
idea.experimental_setup:
Models: SD-1.5, SD-XL-1.0, DiT-XL/2 256, StableVideoDiffusion-XT, StableDiffusion 3-Medium.

Tasks:  • 500 random MS-COCO prompts  • 100 artist-style prompts  • 12 DreamBooth identities  • ControlNet-Canny, ‑Depth, ‑OpenPose (100 images)  • 16-frame text-to-video 512²  • 360-degree panorama generation (new in benchmark).

Solvers: DPM-Solver++ (5 & 8), DEIS-10, HB-GHVB-15; each with and without H3KF.

Baselines: vanilla solver, FasterDiffusion, DeepCache, AdaptiveDiffusion, KaDiR, AsyncDiff (4 GPU), EBFE.

Hardware: single RTX 4090 and mobile RTX 4070 Laptop; energy measured via nvidia-smi and a Yokogawa power analyser.

Metrics:   • latency & kernel launch count  • peak & average VRAM  • FID-50k vs 50-step reference  • sFID heat-maps (8×8 tiles)  • CLIP-Score  • FVD (video)  • KL divergence bound vs observed  • mutual-information budget utilisation  • energy per image (J)  • cache hit ratio.

Ablations:  rank r∈{4,8,16}; β∈{0.2,0.5,1.0} bit/pixel; with / without Koopman basis update; Kronecker vs low-rank diagonal; momentum types (HB, Nesterov, none); 4-bit vs 6-bit cache.
idea.expected_result:
• With only 4 solver steps, H3KF-Diff yields 2.6× (A100) / 2.0× (RTX 4090) speed-up over DDIM-4 and 1.4× over KaDiR, while keeping ΔFID≤0.08 (SD-XL).  
• Under CFG = 14 + ControlNet-Pose, image KL divergence stays below 0.003, and the theoretical bound is tight within 15 %.  
• Memory-elastic caching fits SD-XL in ≤14 GB, enabling real-time generation on an RTX 4070 Laptop (92 ms per 1024²).  
• Mutual-information scheduling reduces key frames by 38 % versus fixed-ε KaDiR.  
• Video experiment: 16-frame 512² clip in 380 ms with FVD 270 (baseline 1000 ms / 280).  
• OpenRT-Diff results show consistent gains across five backbones and verify that error maps correlate with human perceptual judgments (ρ=0.82).
idea.expected_conclusion: H3KF-Diff pushes training-free diffusion acceleration into the extreme 4–5-step regime while giving formal guarantees on image divergence and numerical stability.  By unifying Koopman linearisation, Kronecker-structured Kalman filtering, information-theoretic scheduling, and Bayesian-derived momentum, it converts the UNet into an anytime, uncertainty-aware renderer that fits even laptop-class GPUs.  The public OpenRT-Diff benchmark standardises evaluation of real-time, high-guidance scenarios and will catalyse further research on principled, resource-adaptive diffusion inference for images, video and future 3-D/mobile applications.

idea.open_problems:
A. Existing feature-reuse methods—even with covariance tracking—still treat every prompt in isolation; they cannot exploit the fact that users often issue temporally-adjacent prompts in interactive sessions (e.g., editing a canvas or generating video frames).  Latent trajectories therefore get re-initialised for each request, wasting warm-started statistics and causing bursty latency.
B. GPU/TPU kernels remain launch-bound once the solver reaches <4 steps; even after caching, arithmetic units are idle ~35 % of the time because tensor shapes shrink toward the end of the denoising chain.
C. Current Kalman-style error bounds are derived for Gaussian priors; they do not hold for the heavy-tailed, perceptually-weighted losses (sFID, sFVD) that actually drive human judgement.
D. There is no mechanism for gracefully degrading quality when the device becomes thermally throttled or battery-constrained on mobile hardware.
E. Privacy and bias auditing are absent: feature caches may leak prompt or identity information if reused across sessions.
idea.methods:
We propose DynaDiff-KPG (Dynamic Kernel-Partitioned, Game-Theoretic Koopman–Kalman Graph) – an adaptive, session-aware inference framework that augments H3KF-Diff with three new ideas.
1. Session-Persistent Hyper-Kalman Filter (SP-HKF):   We maintain a ‘hyper-state’ summarising cross-prompt drift in Koopman eigen-space (mean, Kronecker Σ, and spectral drift matrix).  A light 256-parameter GRU updates this hyper-state online and initialises the per-prompt HKF so that successive prompts start from a warm, low-error regime.  This amortises the cost of key frames over a whole session and yields up to 1.4× extra speed-up for interactive UI workflows.
2. Kernel-Fusion Micro-Scheduler:   We formulate the UNet as a dependency DAG and partition it into micro-kernels.  A mixed-integer linear program (solved once per model) packs these kernels into macro-kernels under on-chip SRAM and register-file constraints, maximising arithmetic occupancy in the 32–128 µs regime where launch overhead dominates.  The scheduler is aware of cache hits produced by SP-HKF and can fuse only the still-active kernels, reducing launches by 48 % relative to H3KF.
3. Risk-Sensitive Control via Rényi Bounds:   We generalise the pixel-wise Gaussian KL bound to an α-Rényi bound with α≈0.5, which upper-bounds the expected perceptual divergence under heavy-tailed noise models.  This lets us translate mutual-information budgets (β) into guarantees on sFID/sFVD.  A game-theoretic controller picks the aggressiveness of key-frame skipping subject to (device power × risk) ≤ τ, enabling real-time adaptation to thermal or battery budgets.
4. Secure Cache Isolation Layer:   A per-session randomly keyed SHA-256 tag is stored with each cached tile; tags are invalidated when the user switches tasks or identities, eliminating cross-session leakage while retaining intra-session reuse.
5. Open-Session-RT Benchmark:   We extend OpenRT-Diff with scripted interactive sessions (prompt editing, ControlNet scribbles, video frame interpolation) and provide energy-throttling scenarios on a Pixel 8 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro.

idea.methods:
We propose HYPER-D³ (Heterogeneous, prIvacy-Preserving, Hybrid-Execution, sEssion-aware, Risk-bounded Discrete-Diffusion) – a superset of DynaDiff-KPG that unifies cross-device migration, multi-backbone reuse, micro–macro scheduling and adaptive quantisation.
1.  Cross-Device Hyper-State Replication (CD-HSR) – The SP-HKF state is serialised into a 768-byte Protobuf with per-layer Δ-RLE compression and AES-GCM encryption.  A trust policy decides which subset of the hyper-state (means, low-rank eigenvectors, α-Rényi risk) is allowed to migrate from mobile to cloud or vice-versa.  This lets an AR headset resume generation in 18 ms after off-loading heavy steps to a desktop.
2.  Backbone-Invariant Koopman Adapter – We train a tiny adapter Φl→l′ (128-dim linear map + bias) that projects the hyper-state of SD-XL layers into the latent space of SVD-XT or ControlNet-Depth.  It is fitted on-the-fly with 50 paired key-frames using recursive Least-Squares, costing <2 ms.  Thus one image session can seamlessly branch into video or control-guided tasks without cold-start.
3.  Parareal-Aware Micro-Macro Scheduler – We embed an SRDS-style parareal loop inside the Kernel-Fusion scheduler: coarse 1-step predictions run on the graphics queue while fine  √N-step corrections occupy tensor cores; fused kernels are launched only for the delta blocks that parareal marks ‘uncertain’.  This overlaps memory-bound and compute-bound phases and recovers ~22 % idle SM time.
4.  Quant-Skip Co-Design – Each micro-kernel carries a 4-bit NDTC quantisation plan plus a ‘skip likelihood’ πt from the SP-HKF covariance.  An ILP packs ( quantised-&-cached, quantised-fresh, full-precision-fresh ) variants into SRAM under a bandwidth budget β_bw.  On a Pixel 8 Pro this lowers DRAM traffic by 41 % while keeping sFID drift <0.08.
5.  Fairness-Leakage Monitor – We derive a chi-square test on the per-channel Rényi bound: if the cumulative bound for any protected attribute (gender, skin-tone classifier score) drops below ζ, the cache is force-flushed and the user is prompted.  This yields an (ε,δ)-DP style guarantee over a whole session.
6.  Open Hetero-Session-RT Benchmark – extends Open-Session-RT with device-handoff traces (phone→cloud→headset), backbone switches (image→video) and fairness probes (FAIR-Face subset).  Energy and thermal logs are recorded via Android HAL and Nvidia NVML.

idea.open_problems:
1. Current accelerators either assume a fixed, single-device context or treat device-migration as an all-or-nothing hand-off. There is no fine-grained routing of individual solver steps (or even spatial tiles) to the most suitable processor under constantly-changing bandwidth, thermal and privacy constraints.
2. Existing cross-backbone warm-starts rely on a linear Koopman map fitted on the fly. When the target backbone diverges strongly in architecture (e.g. video diffusion with temporal convolutions, or depth-conditioned ControlNet) a single linear map is often insufficient, forcing re-initialisation and quality loss.
3. Kalman / Parareal feature reuse has so far been exploited only for arithmetic efficiency; the communication cost of sending those reused features across WAN or Bluetooth is now the dominant latency when phones collaborate with cloud or wearables.
4. Quantisation and skipping are still designed at tensor granularity. However, the memory-bandwidth bottleneck on mobile NPUs is dominated by a handful of large attention tiles; no scheduler reasons at tile-level while also accounting for network transfer cost.
5. Current privacy and fairness monitors flush the whole cache when a statistical test fails, which hurts UX. A more surgical mitigation that perturbs only the offending channels or tiles is missing.
idea.methods:
We propose ORCHID-D⁴: Orchestrated, Hierarchical, Differentially-private, Distributed Diffusion.
A. Step-Level Dynamic Off-Loading (SL-DO). We formalise inference as a Mixed-Integer Program that assigns every solver step t and every 32×32 latent tile τ to one of M heterogeneous devices. The objective minimises end-to-end latency plus an energy–privacy regulariser. The cost coefficients are profiled online (using micro-benchmarks and measured network RTT) and the MIP is re-solved every 0.5 s via a warm-started branch-and-bound on the phone’s little cores (≤3 ms).
B. Piece-wise Koopman Adapter (PKA). Instead of one global linear Φ we learn a small dictionary of K piece-wise linear maps {Φ_k}. A decision tree, trained once on open-source backbones and then pruned to 8-KB, selects Φ_k based on layer depth, channel group and condition type. At run-time only the chosen Φ_k is fine-tuned with recursive least squares, preserving cross-backbone reuse even for video or depth branches.
C. Hierarchical Rényi-Coded State (HRCS). The SP-HKF state is entropy-coded with a learnt Gaussian-mixture prior and split into three tiers: (1) 96-byte per-tile mean, (2) optional 4-bit low-rank basis, (3) optional eigen-noise seeds. SL-DO may decide to migrate only tier-1 for slow links (BLE) and reconstruct higher tiers locally with a calibrated noise injector, cutting average transmitted bytes by 4.6×.
D. Tile-Aware Quant-Skip (TAQS). Attention maps are partitioned into 8×8 tiles; each tile carries a skip-probability π and a candidate bit-width b∈{4,8,16}. A bi-criteria knapsack packs tiles into the on-chip SRAM budget while maximising ( expected quality gain − λ·transfer_cost ). TAQS is solved greedily in <0.8 ms and feeds its decision back to SL-DO so that communication and memory trade-offs are globally consistent.
E. Channel-Selective Fairness Noise (CF-Noise). When the chi-square monitor detects over-fitting on a protected attribute, only the top-p offending channels (ranked by Rényi contribution) are reset to fresh Gaussian noise; the rest of the cache stays. This reduces cache flush frequency by 8× while capping leakage at the same δ.
